questions.q: A research platform runs an orchestrator with 12 parallel worker agents. Workers duplicate each other's searches. The architectural fix is:
opts: Orchestrator assigns explicit, disjoint subtask boundaries and a shared task ledger workers consult
questions.exp: At scale, orchestrators must own decomposition: explicit disjoint scopes plus shared state prevent duplicated effort.
why: More workers multiplies the duplication.
Correct. Disjoint subtask boundaries plus a shared ledger stop workers repeating each other.
Free negotiation reintroduces the coordination overhead isolation avoids.
Collapsing to one worker discards the parallelism entirely.

questions.q: When an orchestrator delegates to workers, what should flow back?
opts: Compact structured results (findings, citations, confidence) against the assigned subtask contract
questions.exp: Contract-based handoffs with distilled artifacts keep orchestrator context lean and synthesis tractable.
why: Full transcripts drown the orchestrator in detail.
Correct. Compact structured results against the assigned subtask contract.
Withholding results until the end removes the orchestrator's ability to steer.
Raw tool logs belong with the worker that produced them.

questions.q: You must choose between one agent with 40 tools vs. a router to 4 specialist agents with ~10 tools each. Specialists win mainly because:
opts: Smaller focused tool sets and prompts reduce selection errors and context bloat per query
questions.exp: Tool-selection accuracy degrades as toolsets balloon; specialization keeps each decision space small.
why: Total compute is not the differentiator.
Correct. Smaller focused tool sets reduce selection errors and context bloat.
Diagram aesthetics are not an engineering argument.
Routing costs a classification call; it is not free.

questions.q: A long-horizon agent must survive process restarts mid-task. Professional-grade design:
opts: Keep state only in the context window
Externalize state: durable task ledger/checkpoints so any run can resume from last known-good step
questions.exp: Durable externalized state with checkpointing is how production agents achieve resumability.
why: Context-only state is lost on any restart.
Correct. Externalize state so a run can resume from the last known-good step.
Restarts cannot be prevented, only survived.
Rerunning from scratch wastes all completed work.

questions.q: Which task profile justifies multi-agent parallelization despite ~15x token cost?
opts: Breadth-heavy research where independent subtopics can be explored simultaneously and synthesized
questions.exp: Anthropic's multi-agent research findings: parallel breadth-first exploration is where the cost pays for itself.
why: FAQ answering is a single lookup, not breadth-heavy exploration.
Correct. Independent subtopics explored in parallel and then synthesized.
Formatting is trivially sequential.
One lookup needs no parallel decomposition.

questions.q: An agent's tool starts returning subtly wrong data (not errors). The strongest defense layer is:
opts: Validation checks/invariants on tool outputs in code, with anomalies surfaced to the agent or halting the pipeline
questions.exp: Silent data corruption needs programmatic validation — schema checks, invariants, sanity bounds — not model vigilance alone.
why: Silent corruption is exactly what the model is least able to notice.
Correct. Validate invariants on tool output in code and surface or halt on anomalies.
Prompt length cannot detect wrong data.
Retrying returns the same wrong data.

questions.q: Design a fallback chain for a customer-facing agent when the primary model times out:
opts: Retry with backoff → fallback model tier → cached/templated response → human handoff, with each step logged
Switch to a random provider silently
questions.exp: Layered graceful degradation with observability is the professional reliability pattern.
why: An error page is the outcome to avoid, not the plan.
Correct. Backoff, fallback tier, cached response, then human handoff, each logged.
Infinite retries amplify the outage.
Silent provider switching produces unpredictable behavior and unclear data handling.

questions.q: A batch agent pipeline fails at step 7 of 10 nightly. Rerunning all 10 steps doubles cost. Fix:
opts: Idempotent steps with checkpointed intermediate artifacts so reruns resume at the failure point
questions.exp: Idempotency + checkpoints = cheap recovery. Classic production-agent engineering.
why: Accepting doubled nightly cost ignores an easy fix.
Correct. Idempotent steps with checkpoints let reruns resume at the failure point.
Removing a step changes the result silently.
Running less often does not make the failure cheaper.

questions.q: How should an agent handle ambiguous instructions in a high-stakes workflow?
opts: Detect ambiguity and ask for clarification or route to a human rather than acting on assumptions
questions.exp: Professional systems encode 'when uncertain, clarify or escalate' — silent assumptions cause the worst incidents.
why: Confident guessing in a high-stakes workflow is the failure mode.
Correct. Detect ambiguity and clarify or route to a human rather than assume.
Cost is the wrong tiebreaker for a high-stakes ambiguity.
Blanket refusal removes the capability rather than handling the edge case.

questions.q: A pipeline uses Opus-class for every step including trivial formatting. The optimization is:
opts: Model tiering: route each step to the cheapest model that meets its quality bar, verified by evals
questions.exp: Per-step model routing backed by eval evidence is the canonical cost strategy.
why: Uniformity is not worth paying top-tier rates for formatting.
Correct. Route each step to the cheapest model that meets its quality bar, verified by evals.
Removing quality checks trades correctness for cost.
Formatting steps are usually necessary; the tier is what is wrong.

questions.q: Which lever cuts cost the most for an agent with a large stable system prompt + tools called 100k times/day?
opts: Prompt caching of the stable prefix
questions.exp: At that volume the cached prefix dominates spend — caching stable content is the first lever to pull.
why: Naming saves a negligible number of tokens.
Correct. At that volume the repeated prefix dominates spend, so cache it.
Parallelism changes throughput, not cost per call.
A ten-token output reduction is irrelevant against a large repeated input.

questions.q: Latency-sensitive interactive step + quality-sensitive back-office step. Strategy?
opts: Fast model (streaming) for interactive; stronger model, possibly with extended thinking, for the async step
questions.exp: Match model and inference settings to each step's latency/quality profile.
why: One model cannot be optimal for opposite constraints.
Correct. Optimize each step for its own latency or quality constraint.
Maximum capability everywhere wastes money on the latency-bound path.
Maximum speed everywhere sacrifices the quality-critical step.

questions.q: How should you tune how much Claude reasons on a given class of task?
opts: Always run at the maximum setting
Empirically — set reasoning effort per task class from evals showing where added reasoning actually improves outcomes
Leave it at the default and never revisit it
Turn reasoning off everywhere to save tokens
questions.exp: Reasoning depth is a paid dial, set per task class from evals. On current models the control is the effort level alongside adaptive thinking; the older fixed thinking-token budget has been removed.
why: Maximum effort everywhere multiplies cost and latency for no measured gain.
Correct. Set effort per task class from evals showing where reasoning changes outcomes.
Never revisiting the setting guarantees it is wrong somewhere.
Disabling reasoning entirely degrades the tasks that need it.

questions.q: Before swapping a prompt in a production agent, you should:
opts: Run it against a versioned eval suite of representative and edge cases, comparing to the incumbent
questions.exp: Eval-gated prompt changes are the tested professional norm; vibes are not a regression strategy.
why: Readability is not evidence of behavior.
Correct. Compare against the incumbent on a versioned eval suite before shipping.
A single opinion is not a measurement.
Production is where the cost of being wrong is highest.

questions.q: What belongs in an agent observability stack?
opts: Traces of each step (tool calls, inputs/outputs, tokens, latency), outcome metrics, and sampled human review of transcripts
questions.exp: Step-level tracing plus outcome metrics plus qualitative sampling — you can't fix what you can't see.
why: Error counts miss silent quality failures entirely.
Correct. Step traces, outcome metrics, and sampled human review together.
Host metrics say nothing about agent behavior.
Screenshots do not explain multi-step reasoning.

questions.q: An LLM-as-judge eval disagrees with human raters 40% of the time. You should:
opts: Calibrate: refine the judge rubric against human-labeled examples until agreement is acceptable, or keep humans for that axis
questions.exp: Judge models must be validated against human judgment before being trusted as gates.
why: Cost does not make an unvalidated measurement usable.
Correct. Calibrate the rubric against human labels, or keep humans for that axis.
Deleting the eval leaves no signal at all.
Averaging a calibrated and an uncalibrated source obscures both.

questions.q: Production metrics show quality drift after a model version update. First professional response:
opts: Rerun the eval suite on the new version, identify failing segments, then patch prompts or pin/route models accordingly
questions.exp: Evals localize the regression; then targeted fixes or version pinning — measured response over reflex.
why: A blanket rollback discards the improvements along with the regressions.
Correct. Rerun the evals, isolate failing segments, then patch or pin accordingly.
Ignoring a known regression compounds the damage.
Attribution is not remediation.

questions.q: An agent has email-send and file-delete tools. Governance requires:
opts: Least-privilege scoping, human approval gates for irreversible actions, and immutable audit logs of every action
questions.exp: High-impact tools demand scoped permissions, approvals, and auditability — the security triad for agents.
why: Irreversible external actions always need governance.
Correct. Least privilege, approval gates for irreversible actions, immutable audit logs.
Speed is irrelevant to governance.
Removing logs destroys the audit trail that accountability depends on.

questions.q: Your agent browses arbitrary web content, then can call internal tools. Biggest threat to design against?
opts: Prompt injection from fetched content steering internal tool calls — isolate/sanitize content, restrict tool access in browsing contexts
questions.exp: Untrusted content + powerful tools is the classic injection kill-chain; break it architecturally.
why: Latency is an operational concern, not the security threat.
Correct. Injection from fetched content steering internal tools is the core threat.
Media weight is a performance detail.
Consent dialogs are a nuisance, not the risk to design against.

questions.q: Customer PII flows through an agent pipeline. Professional handling includes:
opts: Data minimization, redaction/masking before model calls where feasible, retention policies, and access controls on traces
questions.exp: Traces are data too: minimize, mask, control access, and set retention — governance covers observability artifacts.
why: Verbatim indefinite logging of personal data is the opposite of good practice.
Correct. Minimize, redact where feasible, set retention, and control access to traces.
Emailing logs spreads personal data further with no controls.
Avoiding documentation makes governance impossible.

questions.q: Who should be able to modify a production agent's system prompt?
opts: Authorized roles via change control (review + eval gate + versioned deploy), like any production code change
questions.exp: Prompts are production configuration: access control, review, evals, versioned rollout.
why: Uncontrolled edits to behavior-defining configuration is a production risk.
Correct. Authorized roles, review, eval gate, and versioned deploy.
Self-modification removes human accountability.
Freezing prompts prevents necessary fixes.

questions.q: An agent completed '95% of the task' then errored. Users got nothing. Improvement?
opts: Design for partial delivery: stream/persist intermediate results so completed work survives failures
questions.exp: Persisting incremental artifacts converts failures into partial successes — a hallmark of production-grade design.
why: Capability does not address the loss of completed work.
Correct. Persist intermediate results so completed work survives a late failure.
Hardware is not the constraint.
Full retries discard the work already paid for.

questions.q: You're scaling from 1 to 50 concurrent agent sessions sharing tools and rate limits. Key addition:
opts: Central concurrency/rate management: queues, per-session budgets, and backpressure so sessions degrade fairly
questions.exp: Shared-resource contention needs queuing, budgets, and backpressure — orchestration at the fleet level.
why: Contention behavior changes fundamentally at fifty concurrent sessions.
Correct. Queues, per-session budgets, and backpressure make degradation fair.
More keys does not create fair scheduling and may breach terms.
Prompt size is unrelated to shared-resource contention.

questions.q: The best eval set for a support agent is built from:
opts: Representative real cases plus curated hard/edge cases and known past failures, refreshed over time
questions.exp: Evals must mirror reality and stress boundaries; stale or easy-only suites give false confidence.
why: Easy synthetic questions measure nothing that matters.
Correct. Real representative cases plus curated hard ones and past failures, refreshed over time.
One transcript cannot characterize a distribution.
Marketing copy is not a workload.

questions.q: An orchestrator spawns workers whose combined output no longer fits in its own context. The right response is:
opts: Increase the orchestrator's context window and continue
Have workers return bounded, schema-constrained summaries, and synthesize in stages if needed
Reduce the number of workers until it fits
Drop the results that arrive last
questions.exp: Bounding what each worker returns is the scalable fix. Growing the window or truncating results only postpones or hides the problem.
why: A larger window raises the ceiling without changing the growth pattern.
Correct. Bound each worker's return and synthesize hierarchically.
Cutting workers sacrifices coverage to work around a format problem.
Discarding by arrival order loses information arbitrarily.

questions.q: A multi-agent design costs many times a single-agent one. That is justified when:
opts: Parallel exploration measurably improves outcomes enough to warrant the token multiple
questions.exp: Multi-agent architectures buy parallel breadth at a large token multiple; the gain must be measured, not assumed.
why: Preference is not a justification for a cost multiple.
Correct. Measured outcome gains must exceed the added spend.
Marketing is not evidence for your workload.
Duration alone does not imply parallel decomposition helps.

questions.q: Subagents in a fleet should generally not coordinate directly with each other because:
opts: Cross-talk destroys the context isolation and parallelism that made the design worthwhile
It is slower to send messages
questions.exp: Isolation is the point: self-contained tasks, fresh context, and results returned to the orchestrator.
why: It is possible, just usually undesirable.
Correct. Cross-talk reintroduces the coupling isolation was meant to remove.
Latency is a secondary concern next to the architectural cost.
Nothing forbids it; the argument is design, not permission.

questions.q: The orchestrator's context in a large fleet should contain:
opts: Compact structured results and the state needed to decide next steps
The full contents of every tool response
questions.exp: The orchestrator needs decisions, not raw transcripts. Aggregating everything recreates the overflow the fan-out avoided.
why: Full transcripts drown the orchestrator in detail.
Correct. Compact results plus decision state is what it actually needs.
Dropping subagent results leaves nothing to synthesize.
Raw tool payloads belong with the subagent that requested them.

questions.q: A fleet's aggregate token usage grows faster than its task volume. The first thing to examine is:
opts: Whether users are asking harder questions
Whether agents are retrying, looping, or re-reading context they already have
questions.exp: Superlinear token growth usually indicates wasted work: retries, loops, and redundant context rather than genuine demand.
why: Possible, but it would generally scale with volume rather than outpace it.
Correct. Retries, loops, and redundant context are the usual causes.
Model changes are deliberate and would be a known event.
Application logging does not consume model tokens.

questions.q: An agent completes ninety percent of a task then fails. Users receive nothing. The design fix is:
opts: Persist intermediate results so a late failure still delivers completed work
questions.exp: Checkpointing converts all-or-nothing failure into partial delivery and gives retries a resume point.
why: Capability does not address the loss of completed work.
Correct. Persist as you go so partial progress survives failure.
Longer timeouts postpone rather than prevent total loss.
Full retries discard the ninety percent already paid for.

questions.q: A nightly ten-step pipeline fails at step seven. The most efficient recovery is:
opts: Resume from step seven using persisted outputs of the earlier steps
questions.exp: Idempotent, checkpointed steps let you resume rather than repeat, which saves both time and spend.
why: Rerunning completed work wastes time and money.
Correct. Resume from the failure point using stored outputs.
Skipping a step changes the result silently.
Duplicate runs multiply cost without addressing the failure.

questions.q: A downstream dependency degrades intermittently under load. The right agent-side behavior is:
opts: Backoff with jitter, a retry ceiling, and a defined fallback when the ceiling is hit
Fail the entire run on first error
questions.exp: Bounded backoff with jitter avoids amplifying an outage, and an explicit fallback keeps behavior predictable.
why: Aggressive retries worsen the degradation for everyone.
Correct. Bounded, jittered retries with a defined fallback.
Failing immediately on a transient error is needlessly brittle.
Ignoring errors yields confidently wrong output.

questions.q: Distinguishing recoverable from unrecoverable failures matters because:
opts: Retrying an unrecoverable failure burns budget and delays surfacing a problem that needs a human
questions.exp: Retry policy should follow failure class. Retrying a permanent error is pure waste and hides the real issue.
why: Any saving is a side effect of not wasting retries.
Correct. Class determines whether to retry or escalate.
Log volume is incidental.
This is application design, not an API requirement.

questions.q: A production agent silently produces lower-quality output after a dependency schema change. This was missed because:
opts: There was no outcome monitoring — only crash-level alerting
Users did not complain loudly enough
questions.exp: Silent quality regressions require outcome-level monitoring; uptime and error rates will not surface them.
why: Models do not silently degrade on their own.
Correct. Without outcome metrics, quality regressions are invisible.
Prompt length is unrelated to detecting regressions.
Relying on complaints means detecting damage after it lands.

questions.q: An interactive step must feel fast and an overnight step must be accurate. The right strategy is:
opts: A fast model with streaming for the interactive step; a stronger model, and more reasoning effort, for the async step
questions.exp: Match model and inference settings to each step's latency and quality profile rather than standardizing on one.
why: A single choice cannot be optimal for opposite constraints.
Correct. Optimize each step for its own constraint.
Uniform maximum capability wastes money on the latency-bound step.
Uniform speed sacrifices quality where quality is the requirement.

questions.q: Latency is dominated by a large fixed prompt resent on every call. The most effective change is:
opts: Cache the stable prefix so repeated content is not reprocessed each time
questions.exp: When a large prefix repeats, caching removes the dominant repeated work.
why: Variable input is the small part of the payload here.
Correct. Caching the stable prefix removes the repeated cost.
Output caps do not address input processing.
Concurrency raises throughput without reducing per-call latency.

questions.q: Deciding whether to move a step to a cheaper model, the deciding evidence should be:
opts: An eval on representative production cases showing quality holds
A colleague's experience on a different task
questions.exp: Substitutions must be validated on your own distribution; price is only meaningful once quality is shown to hold.
why: Price without quality evidence is an incomplete decision.
Correct. Validate on representative cases before switching.
A different task is not evidence for yours.
Recency is not a quality guarantee.

questions.q: Setting reasoning effort per task class rather than globally is preferable because:
opts: Effort is a paid dial and only some task classes convert it into better outcomes
questions.exp: Reasoning depth costs tokens and latency; it should be spent where evals show it changes results.
why: Per-class configuration is more work, not less.
Correct. Spend reasoning where it demonstrably improves outcomes.
Global configuration is possible; it is just wasteful.
Per-class tuning can raise cost where high effort is warranted.

questions.q: The most defensible way to set a per-run budget cap for an agent is:
opts: A round number chosen by the team
The observed cost distribution of successful runs, with headroom, so caps catch runaway behavior rather than normal work
questions.exp: Caps should be derived from observed successful-run cost so they catch pathology without killing legitimate work.
why: An arbitrary number will either be ineffective or cut off valid runs.
Correct. Derive the cap from the real distribution, plus headroom.
The minimum would terminate most legitimate runs.
No cap means a loop can run until someone notices the bill.

questions.q: Your agent's offline evals look healthy but users report worse results. The most likely gap is:
opts: The eval set no longer reflects the production distribution — real traffic has drifted away from it
questions.exp: Evals measure the distribution you built them from. When production drifts and the set does not, healthy scores stop meaning healthy behaviour.
why: Difficulty would depress scores, not inflate them relative to reality.
Correct. A stale eval set measures a distribution that no longer exists.
Dismissing consistent user reports discards your best signal.
Version changes are deliberate events, not silent ones.

questions.q: An agent observability stack should capture:
opts: Step-level traces — tool calls, inputs and outputs, tokens, latency — plus outcome metrics and sampled human review
questions.exp: You cannot debug or improve what you cannot see. Step traces, outcomes, and qualitative sampling cover the three levels that matter.
why: Error counts miss silent quality failures entirely.
Correct. Traces, outcome metrics, and sampled human review together.
UI captures do not explain agent behavior.
The final answer hides where a multi-step run went wrong.

questions.q: The most important property of a regression set used to gate deployments is:
opts: That it is representative of real production cases, including known failure modes
That the current system passes all of it
questions.exp: Representativeness beats size. A set the system already passes entirely provides no signal about the changes that matter.
why: Size without representativeness measures the wrong distribution.
Correct. Mirror production, and deliberately include known failures.
A set you always pass cannot detect regressions.
A constantly changing set makes results incomparable over time.

questions.q: Sampling transcripts for human review remains necessary alongside automated metrics because:
opts: It is required by regulation in all cases
Metrics only measure what you thought to measure; reading transcripts surfaces failure modes you have not encoded
It replaces the need for evals
questions.exp: Qualitative review is how new failure modes are discovered and turned into future metrics.
why: Regulatory requirements vary and are not universal.
Correct. Reading real transcripts reveals unmodeled failure modes.
Human review is more expensive per item, not less.
It complements automated evaluation rather than replacing it.

questions.q: The right time to build evaluation for an agent workflow is:
opts: Before meaningful rollout, so changes can be measured from the start
Only if the team has spare capacity
questions.exp: Without a baseline you cannot tell improvement from regression, which makes every subsequent change a guess.
why: Waiting for an incident means learning the expensive way.
Correct. A baseline before rollout makes every later change measurable.
Evaluation is core engineering, not discretionary.
Prompts change constantly; that is precisely why evals are needed.

questions.q: An agent needs to act on behalf of users in two different customer tenants. The critical isolation requirement is:
opts: Tenant identity enforced at the data and tool layer, so no request can reach another tenant's data regardless of what the model does
A larger context window per tenant
questions.exp: Multi-tenant isolation must hold at the resource boundary. Anything enforced only in the prompt can be defeated by injected content or a reasoning error.
why: Prompt separation is not an access control.
Correct. Enforce tenancy at the data and tool layer, below the model.
Context capacity has no bearing on isolation.
Repeating the run does not create a boundary.

questions.q: An agent fleet reads from a shared knowledge store that any team can write to. The main governance risk is:
opts: Poisoned or unreviewed content silently steering every agent that reads it
questions.exp: A shared, writable grounding source is a high-value injection target; write access needs review just as code does.
why: Storage is a cost concern, not a governance one.
Correct. Unreviewed writes propagate to every consuming agent.
Latency is an operational detail.
Duplication is untidy but not a security risk.

questions.q: Agents act on behalf of users with differing permissions. The correct model is:
opts: Give the agent broad service credentials for simplicity
Have the agent act with the requesting user's effective permissions, enforced server-side
Ask the agent to check permissions itself in the prompt
Grant permissions per tool regardless of user
questions.exp: Authorization must be enforced at the resource, scoped to the actual user. A shared powerful credential turns any injection into privilege escalation.
why: Broad shared credentials make every prompt injection a privilege escalation.
Correct. Enforce the requesting user's permissions server-side.
Prompt-level checks can be overridden by injected content.
User-independent permissions ignore who is actually asking.

questions.q: Audit requirements for an agent that takes consequential actions should include:
opts: Who requested it, what the agent did, which tools ran with which inputs, and what approvals were given
questions.exp: Accountability requires reconstructing the decision: requester, actions, tool inputs, and approvals.
why: The output alone cannot reconstruct how it was reached.
Correct. Requester, actions, tool inputs, and approvals together.
Usage metrics are not an audit trail.
Automation increases rather than removes the need for auditability.

questions.q: A customer asks whether an agent can be given autonomous authority to issue refunds. The right answer is:
opts: Yes, if the prompt says to be careful
It depends on defined limits, approval thresholds, and audit — with irreversible or high-value actions gated by a human
No, agents can never take actions
Yes, if the model is capable enough
questions.exp: Autonomy is a governance decision expressed through limits, thresholds, and gates, not a capability question.
why: Prompt instructions are not an authorization control.
Correct. Define limits and thresholds, and gate high-value or irreversible actions.
Agents routinely take actions within appropriate controls.
Capability does not determine what authority should be delegated.

questions.q: A high-volume agent step is latency-bound rather than cost-bound. The most effective first change is:
opts: Move it to the strongest available model
Move it to a faster model tier and stream, then re-measure before doing anything more elaborate
questions.exp: Latency-bound work is fixed by faster inference and earlier first tokens, then re-measured. Reasoning depth and retries push latency the wrong way.
why: Stronger models are generally slower, which worsens a latency problem.
Correct. Faster tier plus streaming, then measure again before optimizing further.
Retries add latency; they do not reduce it.
More reasoning increases time to answer.

questions.q: An agent needs a credential to call an internal system. The safest handling is:
opts: Put the credential in the system prompt so the agent can use it
Keep the credential in the execution environment behind a tool, so the model never sees the secret itself
Let the agent read it from a shared document
Embed it in the tool description
questions.exp: Secrets should live in the execution layer, not in anything the model can emit. A credential in context can be echoed into output or exfiltrated by injection.
why: Anything in the prompt can be reproduced in output or leaked via injection.
Correct. The tool holds the credential; the model only requests the action.
A readable document spreads the secret further and is equally exposed.
Tool descriptions are supplied to the model and are just as exposed.

cards.b: Professional assumes Foundations knowledge and tests production-scale judgment: fleets of agents, reliability engineering, cost strategy, evals, governance. $175.
Orchestrator owns decomposition into disjoint subtasks; workers return compact structured artifacts; shared ledger prevents duplication.
Externalized durable state + idempotent checkpointed steps → any crash resumes from last known-good point.
Retry w/ backoff → fallback model tier → cached/template response → human handoff. Log every step.
Route each pipeline step to the cheapest model meeting its eval-verified quality bar; reserve top tiers for hard steps.
Prompt caching (stable prefixes) · Batches API (50% off async) · right-sized models per step
Using a model to grade outputs at scale — must be calibrated against human ratings before trusting it as a gate.
Per-step traces (tools, tokens, latency) + outcome metrics + sampled human transcript review.
Untrusted content → model → powerful tools. Break it: sanitize/isolate content, restrict tools in exposed contexts, gate sensitive actions.
Minimize, mask before model calls where possible, control access to traces, enforce retention limits.
Change control: authorized roles, review, eval gates, versioned deploys, rollback plans.
Persist intermediate results as you go — a 95%-done failure should still deliver 95% of the value.

lessons.b:
Professional assumes everything in Architect Foundations — the orchestration pattern ladder, Claude Code workflows, tool/MCP design, context management — as settled knowledge. What's new at this level is scale and consequence: instead of designing one agent for one task, you're designing systems that run continuously, serve many users concurrently, cost real money at volume, and fail in front of customers if something goes wrong.

The shift in mindset

Foundations-level thinking asks 'does this architecture work?' Professional-level thinking asks 'does this architecture keep working at 100x the load, survive a bad model response, stay within budget, and produce an audit trail when something goes wrong?' Nearly every Professional domain is a Foundations concept re-examined under the added pressures of scale, cost, and accountability: orchestration becomes multi-agent fleet management, tool design becomes tool security and governance, context management becomes reliability engineering.

How to study for this level

Because Professional questions are scenario-based and assume you already know the Foundations material cold, the highest-leverage prep is: (1) make sure Foundations concepts are second nature, then (2) for each Professional domain, ask yourself 'what specifically breaks about the Foundations-level approach once this runs continuously, in production, at scale?' That question is essentially the exam.

📺 Watch first
▶How Anthropic Built a Multi-Agent AI Research System + Tips for Your OwnA real production system that hits nearly every Professional-level theme: cost, reliability, orchestration at scale.▶Anthropic Workshop: Build Agents That Run for HoursLong-running agent design — directly relevant to reliability, checkpointing, and resumability.
Key takeaways
  • Professional = Foundations concepts re-examined under scale, cost, and accountability pressure.
  • For every domain, ask: what breaks about the simple approach at production scale?
  • Solid Foundations knowledge is a prerequisite, not a separate topic to relearn.

Professional-level architecture is about what changes when you go from one agent to a fleet.

The ledger prevents duplicate work; lean handoffs keep orchestrator context cheap.

What changes at scale

  • Decomposition discipline: an orchestrator coordinating many parallel workers must assign explicit, disjoint subtask boundaries — without a shared task ledger, workers duplicate each other's work (e.g., duplicate searches in a research system)
  • Lean handoffs: workers should return compact, structured results (findings, citations, confidence) against their assigned subtask contract — not full raw transcripts, which balloon orchestrator context and cost
  • Specialization beats a mega-agent: a router to several specialist agents, each with a focused ~10-tool set, produces fewer tool-selection errors and less context bloat than one agent juggling 40 tools
  • Resumability: long-horizon agents need durable, externalized state (a task ledger/checkpoints) so a process restart resumes from the last known-good step instead of starting over

When parallelization is worth the cost: breadth-heavy, independently-explorable work (e.g., broad research) is where multi-agent parallelism's extra token cost (Anthropic's own research cites roughly 15x) pays for itself; it's a poor fit for simple or narrow tasks.

Worked example
A market-research system asked to profile 8 competitors dispatches one worker per competitor, each returning a 200-word structured summary with citations. The orchestrator synthesizes 8 summaries (~1,600 words) instead of 8 full research transcripts (~20,000+ words) — the same insight at a fraction of the context cost.

Anthropic's own published research on their multi-agent research system is worth internalizing in detail: they found token usage alone explains roughly 80% of the variance in performance across agent configurations, that multi-agent systems excel specifically at breadth-first queries where parallel exploration beats sequential depth, and that the coordination overhead of getting orchestration right (prompt engineering the orchestrator, preventing duplicate work, synthesizing cleanly) is nontrivial engineering effort in its own right — not a solved problem you get for free by adding more agents.

Production agent systems are judged on how they fail, not just how they succeed.

Graceful degradation chain for a primary-model timeout or failure.

Key failure modes and defenses

  • Silent corruption vs. loud errors: a tool returning subtly wrong data (not an exception) is more dangerous than an outright failure — defend with programmatic validation, invariants, and sanity bounds on tool outputs, surfaced to the agent or halting the pipeline, rather than trusting the model to notice
  • Idempotency and checkpointing: when a multi-step batch pipeline fails partway through, idempotent steps with checkpointed intermediate artifacts let a rerun resume at the failure point instead of redoing (and repaying for) completed work
  • Handling ambiguity: in high-stakes workflows, an agent encountering ambiguous instructions should detect that and ask for clarification or escalate to a human — not silently guess and act
  • Partial delivery: persist intermediate results as the agent works, so a failure at 95% still delivers 95% of the value instead of nothing
Common mistake
A single retry-or-fail branch with no fallback tier, no cached response, and no human path. One transient timeout then takes down the whole user-facing feature instead of degrading gracefully.

Reliability engineering for agents borrows heavily from classical distributed-systems practice, just applied to a probabilistic component instead of a deterministic one: circuit breakers stop hammering a failing dependency, timeouts prevent one slow call from blocking everything behind it, bulkheads isolate failures so one bad tenant or task type can't take down the whole system, and health checks decide when a fallback path should activate versus recover. The novelty with agents isn't the reliability patterns themselves — it's that the 'service' you're protecting against can fail in semantically weird ways (a technically successful response that's subtly wrong) that classical monitoring wasn't built to catch.

At scale, cost and latency decisions are architecture decisions, made with evidence rather than intuition.

Model tiering per pipeline step, verified by evals rather than guessed.

The core strategies

  • Model tiering: route each step of a pipeline to the cheapest model that meets that step's quality bar — verified with evals, not guessed — reserving top-tier models for the steps that actually need them (using Opus-class for trivial formatting is the textbook anti-pattern)
  • Prompt caching at volume: for a large, stable system prompt/tool set called at high frequency, caching the stable prefix is the single biggest cost lever available
  • Matching inference settings to the step: latency-sensitive interactive steps want a fast model (often streamed); quality-sensitive async/back-office steps can afford a stronger model, possibly with a higher reasoning effort setting

Reasoning effort should be set empirically, per task class, based on evals showing where the added reasoning actually improves outcomes — not maxed out everywhere by default.

At meaningful scale, cost strategy and reliability strategy start to overlap: a fallback model tier (used for graceful degradation) can double as a cost-saving default for lower-priority traffic, and caching (used for cost) also reduces latency, which improves the user-facing reliability of interactive steps. Professional-level architects design these levers together rather than optimizing cost and reliability as separate, uncoordinated efforts — the same infrastructure investment often pays off on both fronts at once.

You can't manage what you can't measure — this domain is about building the feedback loops that let a production agent system improve safely.

No single pillar is sufficient alone — traces without outcomes, or metrics without human sampling, both miss real problems.

The evaluation discipline

  • Eval-gated changes: before shipping a prompt or model change to a production agent, run it against a versioned eval suite of representative and edge/failure cases and compare to the incumbent — 'it reads better to me' is not a regression strategy
  • What good eval sets look like: built from real representative cases plus curated hard/edge cases and known past failures, refreshed over time — not synthetic easy questions or a single demo transcript
  • LLM-as-judge: using a model to grade outputs at scale must be calibrated against human-labeled examples until agreement is acceptable before it's trusted as a gate — an uncalibrated judge is worse than no automated eval

Responding to drift: if quality metrics drop after a model version update, the professional response is to rerun the eval suite to localize which segments regressed, then patch prompts or pin/route model versions accordingly — not blanket panic-rollback or ignoring it.

A mature eval program usually has three layers running at different cadences: fast unit-style checks on every prompt/code change (does the output still parse, does it still pass basic sanity rules), a fuller eval suite run before any production deploy (the representative + edge-case set discussed above), and slower, ongoing production monitoring (sampled human review, outcome metrics, drift detection) that catches things the pre-deploy suite didn't anticipate. Relying on only one layer — especially only the pre-deploy suite — is a common gap; real-world traffic reliably surfaces cases no eval set fully covers.

The final domain covers what changes when agents have real permissions and touch real (often sensitive) data.

The dashed line — untrusted content trying to trigger a sensitive action directly — is exactly what the approval gate exists to stop.

Governance essentials

  • The security triad for high-impact tools: least-privilege scoping, human approval gates before irreversible actions, and immutable audit logs of every action taken
  • The injection kill-chain: untrusted content (arbitrary web pages, emails) flowing into a model that can then call powerful internal tools is the classic attack path. Break it architecturally — sanitize/isolate untrusted content, restrict which tools are reachable in browsing/exposed contexts, and gate sensitive actions behind approval
  • PII handling: minimize what flows through the pipeline, mask/redact before model calls where feasible, control access to traces (traces are data too), and enforce retention limits — governance extends to your observability artifacts, not just the primary data
  • Prompts as production config: treat system-prompt changes to a production agent like any other production code change — authorized roles, review, eval gates, versioned deploys, and a rollback plan

Concurrency at scale: scaling from one session to many concurrent agent sessions sharing tools and rate limits requires central concurrency management — queues, per-session budgets, and backpressure — so sessions degrade fairly under load instead of starving each other.

Key takeaways
  • Least privilege + approval gates + audit logs is the non-negotiable baseline for high-impact tools.
  • Untrusted content and powerful tools must never mix without an isolation boundary.
  • Prompts, like code, need change control once they're in production.

It's worth naming the underlying tension explicitly: every capability you give an agent (browsing the web, writing to a database, sending communications, spending money) is simultaneously what makes it useful and what makes it dangerous if misdirected — by a bug, a bad prompt, or an injection attack. There's no configuration that eliminates this tension; governance is the discipline of consciously choosing, for each capability, how much value it's worth versus how much blast radius you're willing to accept, and building the guardrails (scoping, approval, audit) proportional to that choice rather than uniformly everywhere or nowhere.
